The monetary crisis which has been so se- I verely felt, not only in this country, but throughout Europe and America, is of such recent occurrence that there lias not yet been time to ascertain what effect it will have upon the þÿhank business, s but the directors do not entertain any apprehension that it can be serious ; whilst ou the other hand they cannot Hatter themselves that the hank will escape I loss. In the meantime they have much satis faction in reporting that every ascertained loss has been provided for. and that they will he able fully to meet any doubtful contingencies which may arise from recent events, without interfering with either the dividend or tinsteady increase of the reserved fund, of which the foundation has been laid this day. The Chairman said the report which had just been read was not quite so favourable as some of those of past years, hut it confirmed what he took the liberty of anticipating at the last meeting, that they would wipe off the had debts and lay the foundation for a reserved fund (cheers) ; hut recent events made it not quite so large as could have been wished. With regard to the losses, no person except those who had been asleep during the last two months could he so sanguine as to expect they would entirely escape ; however, considering the intensity of the pressure, they had escaped uncommonly well. (Hear j In the spring of the year, when an extraordinary rise took place in the price of sugar and other produce, instructions were sent out to the managers to he

very careful, and not to be led away by speculation ; these had been strictly followed, and out of hills amounting to 1,300,000/ , all had been paid within 8000/., which were returned, and might yet he recovered. They had also had considerable remittances through the United States, all of which had come to hand with out injury to the bank, so that upon the whole he considered they could not he otherwise than satisfied, as the severe test proved the soundness of the business. The bank hail gone through some reverses ; hut the had debts, which at one time stood at 210,000/ , hud all been paid off, while the shareholders had received dividends averaging for the last five years at least 4J per cent. : and their shares, which at one time were down to 5, now stood at 20, and before the crisis were at 30. Looking, therefore, at the crisis they had passed through, lie thought their position was very favourable ; he, therefore, begged to move the adoption of the report. Mr. IIelmk congratulated the meeting on the state of their affairs after the ordeal they had gone through the last half-year, and through the exertions of the directors they had wiped off all the bad debts, and founded a reserve fund. (Hear.) The Chairman next proposed that a dividend at the rate of 3/. per cent, for the halfyear be declared, payable on and after Jan. 12. A vote of thanks to the Chairman terminated the proceedings.

In India single provinces exceed in dimensions powerful European States ; separate district are measured by thousands of square miles, and the aggregate population of the Empire is reckoned by hundreds of millions. Nor is this population deficient in warlike elements, for ir Oude alone our Commauders are confronted I by an armed mass which nobody computes at 18 84 j ! is an extreme case, less tliau 60,000 fighting men. This, it is tru". since the province of Oude 10 31 ! is botii more densely peopled and more martially disposed than any other in India ; but there arc few districts iu which a promising foray or a successful revolt may not attra. t its thou sands of marauders, tolerably well equippt'C and hereditarily addicted to the pursuits of war The natural conclusion would be that in a country like tins any moderate efforts would go for nothing, and that our battallioos of 700 or 800 men would be lost like drops in the been esta blished. Nevertheless, at every turn aud phasof th ; contest we have found its whole course influenced by bodies of troops so small a to be distinguishable in the mm around them. FRANCE. M. Vriere, the Belgian Minister of Foreign Affairs, has written a dispatch to the Ambassador of Belgium, in Paris, promising to expel every refugee whom the French Government might name, and to keep the other refugees under the strictest control. It is stated that the French Government is determined to take, if necessary, a decided part in the affairs of the extreme East, and that the plan of an expedition on a large scale is in contemplation. It is even arranged that the French troops shall pass through Egypt, and that Admiral Rigault de Genouilly shall meet them at Suez with his fleet. But before this plan is carried into execution, the Emperor will wait for the capture of Canton, and the dispatches from Baron Gros as to the state of ' affairs. It is said to be finally settled that Count Walcwski is to resign the Ministry of Foreign j Affairs, and kgo to London as ambassador, Count de Persiguy returning to Paris, in order to take his seat in the new Privy Council. In this case the new Minister for Foreign Affairs will be M. Drouyn de Lhuys, who has lately dined three times with the Emperor. He, ns is well known, is one of the most honourable and independent men that the Emperor ever had in his service. The_ Pays contains an article which endeavours to prove that the revival of the slave trade, called free emigration by the French Government, is one of the most useful measures which the Emperor could conceive ; for King Dahomey, who formerly slaughtered thousands
of prisoners because be could turn them to no account, andjdid not clioose to be burdened by them, now spared his prisoners, and delivered them to the French Commissioners of free emigration.

It is stated that orders have been given that no more addresses from the army should be published in the Monitewr, in or French French paper published in any other and in France. The news that Marshal Vaillant gives up the Ministry of War to General Neil is confirmed. There are good reasons for supposing that the Duke of (Malakoff is appointed Commander-in- Chief of (the Army of Paris, in the place ot Magnan, and that the latter will be sent as to St. Petersburg.)

The Royal nuptials celebrated on Monday last have doubtless had the effect of prolonging that special attention which lias of late been generally directed to the subject of marriage. There remains, perhaps, not much more to be said on the question of matrimony contracted on ,£300 a-year ; to which the fact of a marriage whereupon the parties have ventured on the strength of £8,000 per annum and upwards seems to have little relation. The match which came off on Monday was at least not an imprudent one with respect to the main chance. No difficulties about housekeeping are likely to destroy or diminish the domestic bliss of the young Prince and Princess of Prussia. Their niuturul felicity, barring unforeseen misfortunes, which it is to be hoped will never happen, rests with themselves ; depends on the inclination and the ability of each to make the other happy. Neither the inclination nor the ability are doubted in their case ; but in that, as well as in every other, the ability must accompany the inclination. The inclination by no means necessarily implies the ability ; and there are other prudential considerations to be regarded in tho contemplation of marriage than those which relate merely to property and income. The mere certainty of three meals a day, and animal comforts, will render a pair of married partners no happier than the same circumstances would make a couple of pigs,

Bad tempers and opposite tastes may convert the state of matrimony into precisely the reverse of a paradise on earth. Practically, however, moral character has some thought taken about it by the majority of persons about to marry ; the union of the vixen with the brute is not a very frequent occurrence, and wedlock does not generally resemble perdition. But if moral wealth is taken somewhat into account, little or no regard whatever is in many cases paid to intellectual competence. The consequence is that the married life of an exceedingly large number of persons becomes, not utterly miserable, but deplorably dull and dreary ; not a terrestrial state of torment, indeed, but a grievous bore. All the comfort and pleasure, specifically human, which married folks can impart to each other, are communicated by talk, and what must that be if there are no ideas to interchange? It lias long been known that the moon revolves on its axis in the same time in which it revolves round the earth, and that it consequently always presents nearly the same side towards the earth, while the opposite side is never seen from our globe. No bodies of water nor clouds can be seen on the moon by the aid of the most powerful telescope, nor is the apparent direction of stars close to its edge changed by refraction, as would be the case if an atmosphere enveloped the moon. Hence it has been inferred by Whcwell, the reputed author oi t l it work entitled : " Of Plurality of Worlds," that the moon has no atmosphere or water, and consequently, no inhabitants. This influence is shown to be inconclusive by a iv e in discovery of the astronomer Hansel, whose study of the moon's motion, continued for many years, has nblished i .c fact that the centre of gra- > no e li than it is from the other . rth. at the centre of figure, is be- ,.mt:e, and farther from the side .noon, instead of being like that s ; Ay-four miles. The nearer side of the moon cannot be inhabited, at least by beings to whose existence air and water are essential, as is the case with all terrestrial animals.

The late celebrated mathematician, Gauss, proposed, as a means of settling the question whether the moon is inhabited, that a huge monument should be erected on the steppes of Siberia, as a signal to the inhabitants of the moon, in the hope that they might be induced to erect a similar signal, to apprise us of their existence. The discovery of Hansel shows that such an experiment could be attained with no success, inasmuch as the inhabitants of the moon, if there are any, being on the further side, could never see a monument on the earth. þÿ Huston Courier.

" The now year opens ominously for Mexico ; the whole country is in a state of convulsion, ami great changes arc hourly expected to take place. In consequence of the pronunciamiento' on the. 17th of Deeemher, several provinces, rather their Governors, declaicd vio- or lent opposition to that scheme of Government. It was natural to suppose they would do so, for in the former state of affairs each Governor was a petty sovereign in his own province, and each little Congress just as full of its own importance an authority as the big Congress in the capital, and, as a matter of course, tho multitude of offices, with handsome salaries thus established, added great attraction to such a system. (In the other hand, Comonfort finds himself to a certain degree isolated, and, though he might derive great elements of success from the general discontent created by the ve,ry system which he has just upset, it is doubted if he will be able to keep his stand, simply bocause he seems incapable of adopting and car rying out any decisive measures. His favourite

tactics consist in coaxing every party and every individual, and being true to none. Thus it is that the " Puros," or ultra -Liberals, who were his associates in power but a few weeks siuee, are now his sworn enemies, and are said to be making great efforts to drive him out of the palace, and to rule in his place. Were they to sueceed, the immediate consequence would be the seizure of the church property, the golden dream of that party. The Santanistas (Santa Anna's partisans) are no less eager to take advantage of the critical state of affairs to bring back their chief once more, and it is said that the latter had promised to be ready in the Havannah during the early part of last month. The ' Conservadores,' made up of the clergy, landed proprietors, and people in affluence generally, would be equally glad to have it all their own way ; but they form a set eminently distinguished in the country for sloth, apathy, and egotism ; consequently tliay are sure to derive no advantage from the influence they really possess, and to remain as helpless as ever, the natural victims of every kind of Government, no matter what its political tenets may be. " Such is the deplorable condition of Mexico just now. It amounts to real anarchy, or rather to a state of confusion difficult to con ceive. The roads, as usual, are infested bv bands of robbers in every direction, nay. even at the very gates of the capital, for the assault upon Mr. Lettsam, Her Majesty's Charge d'Af faires, took place within a very short distance

from the town, and similar exploits have become of every day occurrence. A fresh scene of murder and horror has just taken place in the. tierra caliente' similar to the San Vicente affair. A band of robbers, said to be 60 strong, attacked three 'haciendas' successively, and in one of them most inhumanly killed a Spaniard, as it would appear, simply because he was a Spaniard. A venerable old man, well known in that district for his respectable character and lengthened years (M. Ozante), likewise a Spa niard, was severely beaten, and had a ver\ narrow escape. The whole of the I'nited States correspondence brought by the last steamer from Aew Orleans was robbed before reaching 1'uebla, but has just been recovered " Everything seems to announce some great change as quite imminent ; nor would it ban been reasonable to expect any Mexican Go vernment to last more than i couple of years. only ' ' isset ; iiome that could haTc given it natural to suppose it may be productive of some Whatever that change may happen to be, it is good, simply because nothing could be wnnie than the present state of affairs, particularly with regard to trade. peculiar prerogatives to trample upon every principal of right and wrong. It is considered by them as a great hardship to pay their debts, nor do they blush to traffic with their own dishonour, maintaining that it is quite lawful and proper to curtail the amount of their debts, otto buy them up at the market price, which in all cases is extremely low, as the natural eon sequence of nonpayment and of their proverbial course of dishonesty. Such infamous conduct involves questions of great magnitude for the numerous class of bondholders at home ; indeed, their case may be considered as a hopeless one unless Her Majesty's Government is induced tc interfere in a much more decided manner "

ST. VINCENT AND ST. LUCIA. We have received St. Vincent and St. Lucia papers to the 25tli. A shock of earthquake was felt on the morning of the 24th, at both Islands, without damage. The reaping of the crop was proceeding favorably in St. Vincent, and two vessels, the Spheroid and Florist, had left with sugar for London, and the brig James nearly ready to leave. Two abandoned sugar estates, the Golden Grove and Mount llope, are offered for sale on the 22nd May next, at the Court House, Kingston, under the provisions of the Encumbered Estates' Act. In St. Lucia the quarter of Souffriere was thrown into alarm and disturbance by incendiary fires on the estate of M. Daubeuque, and absurd stories in connexion with the recent death of the Abbe Nicoud, who had committed suicide. It was believed by the ignorant people to have been caused by the agency of the Devil ; and depositions, on oath, are said to have been taken of an interview between certain persons and the Devil. The interference of the Civil Power is invoked tor the protection of life and property, amongst a population led away by the grossest superstition, combined with mischievous propensities.

THE WEST INDIES. It has become evident that we are on list eve of another Anti-Slavery struggle in this country. The gauntlet lias been thrown down in the name of the West India body, and a contemporary declares itself the champion of West India interests. Not that it advocates any very definite plan of promoting them. It does not appear to have yet made up its mind on this point. Just now it is rather in favour of coolie immigration. Vet a few days ago it was a decided partisan of immigration from Africa It would seem, however, that the recent revelations of the true character of this mode of obtaining labour bave, to soinesiiiall extent, modified its views, for it now admits "that if once blacks were known to be wanted, and to be saleable on the coast for some sort of price, they would forthwith be kidnapped for consignment by their own chiefs ; a proceeding which would revive ail the horrors of internal war, and dissipate the chances of improvement which honest traffic is beginning to yield." Herein lies, in fact, the main objection to the West India scheme of so called free African immigration. But this same taper w as not only the last to point out its dangers, but was foremost in its advocacy of it, in spite of the means of information it bad at command, and of communications from competent quarters, showing what was to be apprehended froin raising a demand for men on the African coast. On one point the West India advocates leave the public in no doubt. They demand

immigrant labour for the West Indies. To prove that it is required, they abuse the abolitionists of this country, declare that emancipation lias proved a failure, that the West Indies are ruined, and that their population is steeped iti barbarism, brutality, and indolence. We do not intend, on this occasion, to discuss at any length the, question of immigration. To avoid being misunderstood, however, let us say that to a perfectly free immigration from countries where labour is in abundance to those where it is in greater demand, we see no possible objection. But this is not the kind of immigration demanded by the West India body, and by its pleaders. When the of employ er of labour possesses the power fixing

its price, irrespective of its value, that is. of establishing an arbitrary scale of wages for an arbitrary quantity of work, as the employers conies foreigner of coolies have, the immigrant at once under a system which, in its essential features, resembles the opposition of the friends of free labour. When our own countrymen emigrate they carrv their labour to an open market, and there, like every other raw material, it commands its price, which is regulated by the law of supply and demand, and is subject to the fluctuations incidental thereto. Ifut even during the greatest dearth of labour in our Australian colonies, the wild scheme was never broached of importing labourers from Great Britain as the West India body propose to import coolies from India, China, and Africa ; and we venture to say that, if our countryineu found themselves subject to the same arbitrary regulations as the coolies are, with respect to the standard of wages, tbev would not care to exchange conditions with the immediate prospect, moreover, of a tedious journey across sea, on short rations, and ill-ventilated vessels. We are told that "the negro himself, though lie has become free, has not become wise or industrious. Our planters have not found that free blacks make good la bourers. Negroes are free but they are also brutalised. The West Indies have been ruined. Immense tracts of the most productive soil in the world are The tivated for the want of labour. left uncul- emancipated negro will do can West. India squatter no work at all. The vegetate in abso-

lute idleness, without compulsion or enticement to employ his faculties in work." These are broad and bold statements, and, were they true, would present a discouraging picture of the results of emancipation. But they are not true. Long before emancipation, West India estates were not paying. Even at this day, in Dutch Guiana, where slavery is flourishing, the proprietors are demanding emancipation because the sy stein of slavery is ruinous. It has now become with them a mere question of compensation. If some estates in our colonies are struggling, it is because they are irretrievably mortgaged, and cannot free themselves from the incubus of the London merchant. But we affirm, upon the best authority, that no encumbered properties in all parts of the West Indies arc doing well, a lid their owners making money; that estates worked by free labour produce double the crops they used to do under the system of slavery ; and that the value of land has been and is steadily rising. With respect to the peasantry, we also assert that, as a body, they are neither indolent. brutal, nor uneducated, but that since emancipation they have made advances morally, socially, and religiously, and are steadily progressing. In British Guiana two thirds of them are landed proprietors, according to the last official report of the Registrar of that colony, where squatt eg obtains to a greater extent than in a y other, because there are here vas' back lands for such of the people to occupy tr:

the bad legislation of the plantocracy has driven away from the more inhabited districts. With respect to the products of the colonies, if Jamaica has fallen off in her exports, Barbadoes lias more than doubled hers, and St. Kitts, St. Vincent, and Trinidad are rapidly following in her footsteps. Even British Guiana is progressing in the same direction, though, like Jamaica, it stands in quite a peculiar position, which ii would require more space than we have now at, command to elucidate. One test of the improved physical and social condition of the people is the amount they consume of imported articles. Now, all our West India colonies exhibit a striking improvement in this respect. If. therefore.

f & & Oj (j x K I S , as is the case, the peasantry consume more imported commodities of all kinds than it sed to do, and that the imports show ;:eady increase 011 the whole, it is clear that the people must possess larger means t of expenditure ; and whence are these derived if not from their labour V It is simply a calumny to alledge that the negro is indolent. but it is one of the most malevolent kind. þÿ Evening Slav, January 1.

I'APAL STATES A letter from Vienna dated the 8th inst., which appeared in the Gazette dc la Bourse, of Berlin, states that it had been agreed Rome time since between the Austrian Government and the Pope that the troops of occupation should evacuate the Papal dominions as soon as a native armed force should have been organised and sufficiently trained, and that financial reforms should he introduced. The mo-

ment was drawing near; but the recent at tempt renewed the fears of his Holiness. In consequence, the Court of Rome has declared to the Count Colloredo, that not only is the prolongation of the sojourn of our troops for some time longer absolutely necessary, but that it would even be very desirable to raise them to their former number. (From the Correspondent of the Times.) Paris, Thursday, February 25, 6 þÿp.m. Although it was generally known that the As size Court would be accessible to no one who was not provided with a ticket, or at least that the space reserved for ordinary spectators would be extremely restricted, and that the chances of admission were very slight indeed, yet neither that nor the intense cold prevented crowds from moving in a continuous stream towards the Palace of Justice from the early hour of seven this morning. At nine o'clock preciscly thc doors were thrown open. So continuous was the flow that in less than half an hour the large court was almost full, and after half-past nine the loiterers, however distinguished they might be by the external sign of rank, were unable to get further than the door in spite of the goodwill of the doorkeepers. At a quarter past teu the prisoners were introduced. Each was led by two gendarmes, and were placed in order after each other þÿ Orsini, Rudio, Pierri, and Gomez. Their appearance, as might be expected, drew off atten tion from every other object to fix it on them Every eye-glass and opera-glass was directed to the bench of the accused, and particularly to Orsini. The prisoners were dressed in blackbut this was the only resemblance between them. Of the four, Orsini is certainly the most worthy of remark. He is of middle stature, rather stout, full in face, as in body. Without being what may be called distingue his bearing at all events contrasts with that of his onmp:.

nions, and gives him the air of a man ot the superior classes, lie wore neither beard n" moustache, but only whiskers. If he4woro i white neckcloth instead of a black one be wour be taken for an advocate or an uruue, or .-n employe of the upper ranks. I)c Rudio is of lesser stature than Orsini. an his features are as pinched as those of the other are full. With the exception of a thin mou staehc, his face was clean shaven. Ilis face might in other times have been well-favoured, but his vagrant and wild existence, and vice, or suffering, or both, have effaced whatever traces of distinction or regularity it might have originally possessed. His long hair fell upon his shoulders, and was parted in the fashion of hairdressers' journeymen or apprentices. Gomez certainly has the closest resemblance to the menial servant he personated in the con spiracy. In the first coffee-house or first hotel you enter you may meet visages like his by the dozen. AVhen the prisoners were seated, and the President of the Court was seen to put his first questions to the prisoners (the buzz deep silence succeeded to the interrogatoire), which followed their appearance. These questions were of birth, profession, &c. After purely formal, as to their name, this surname, place was gone through, the prisoners were removed, and the operation of drawing for the jury took place. In about a quarter of an hour the proceedings were resumed. The reading of the acte d'' accusation, which lasted until nearly twelve o'clock, was listened

to with the greatest attention, but the report of Dr. Tardieu, which states that the number of wounded was 156, and the wounds 511, created a profound sensation. When the acte d'accusation was read, the list of witnesses was called over. The emaciated appearance of several of those persons, many of whom are still forced to use crutches, created a very painful sensation in the court. The examination of the prisoners then began. Gomez was the first examined. We have already seen from the indictment that this man made a full confession of the crime ; though in this confession he porsisted to-day, yet what he said was occasionally marked by contradiction and reserve. On coming to the date of the 1 4th of January, he admitted that he was at Orsini's house at 6 p.m. when the final meeting of the conspirators was held, that he had served them with mulled Bordeaux wine, that he had gone out with them having a bomb and a revolver in his possession which had been given to him by Orsini ; but at the same time lie declared that he was completely ignorant of what ho was to do with the projectile or weapon, and if he Hung the bomb under the Emperor's carriage he only obeyed his master's orders. The examination of Rudio then commenced. Rtidio had also made a complete confession, and he on this occasion repeated it. While Rudio was in England, notwithstanding his being a professor of languages, he was nearly starving. He was in this position when he met Bernard, to whom he applied for employ-

ment, and who promised to procure him some. 1'ierri, to whom Bernard recommended him. promised him .'536 francs, and 2s. a week for his wife, if he would follow him to Paris, which he did, and when there he told him what he w as to do. The matter appeared to liim to be tooeerious, but he found himself committed, and his amour propri would not permit him to recede. Orsini was then interrogated The President : You first made admissions, and then you retracted them. Finally, on the »th of February, you addressed a letter to the Attorney-General, in which you protest your innocence. Grsini: I have in fact an explanation to give I have long endeavoured to effort the independence of my country, and this idea has occupied my inind without any feeling of hatred against France being mixed up with it All my hatred was against the Austrians, who since 1816 have never ceased to persecute and plunder us. 1 have never ceased to struggle against Austrian domination, and this is the only crime of which I have been guilty. In 1848 1 hoped with all taly that the end of Austrian domination had arrived A constituent assembly having been convoked at Rome, 1 was elected to form part of it. There, seeing a French army landed, we thought it came as a friend, but when we saw it came as an enemy, we were painfully astonished. An engagement having placed a certain number of French soldiers in our hands, we took advantage of an armistice which the French General accorded to us to restore him his prisoners. The sur-

render took place at the advanced posts to the cry of" Vive la France V' Vive IV Italie At a later period everyone knows how the engagements, the promises, and the armistice were kept. But in spite of that, the political men who then directed affairs at Rome did not cease to show attachment towards France, so persuaded were we all that that war was the act of the government and not of the nation. I he President: The freedom allowed to the defence ought to make us tolerate such words ; but we will revert to them

l\ a e a i i k y i. s , Orsini : Be it so ; but if I be allowed to explain, I shall do so with the same moderation as 1 have hitherto shown. To return to our sentiments towards France, I will say we consider her as so foreign to what passed at Rome, that in all the conspiracies which have taken place at Rome since the duration of the occu-

given that in case of executions or in case of success the French army should be spared. The fall of the Roman Republic becomiug an ! tion was rather a laborious accomplished fact, I have not ceased to labour for the liberation of my country. Instead of placing myself, as Mazzini, in the way of conspiracies which sends out a score or so of armed men in the street, where they are stupidly shot down, 1 wished at first to pursue my object by legal means. When in England 1 wrote and

vention. I applied to the authorities, and I addressed petitions to the Queen for the same purpose. Seeing that all those steps ended in nothing, the faith I had in my cause urged me ! to find out the reasons of my failure. I will not now detail the reasons which convinced me I that the Emperor Napoleon has an interest

Italy. Once convinced that this was the great stumbling-block to our independence, I confess that I resolved to kill him. I say this frankly. I should have preferred executing this design alone, but close access to the Emperor was not easy, and I was therefore obliged to seek associates. After having approved iny plans and given their consent and assistance these men i abandon me to-day, and it is their testimony which has led to my capture by you I will not show reprisals 1 will not recriminate ou them. I pardou them, and 1 offer my li. as a sacrifice to my couutry. Before my judges 1 will only occupy myself with one thing þÿ iy character. Let me nut he judged by the e durations of these men. I do not accuse tin But fear, » liich is a dangerous counsellor, forced on them a system of allegations vn. ch are not in conformity with the truth, 'i ue regard which I liavc for the guilty sufficient explains what iny conscience prescribes tow ai an innocent person. Mr. Allsop is pursued an accomplice. Well, then, 1 am bound to sav that Mr. Allsop has never had any knowledge of this project of assassination. He assisted me in the making of the bombs, in the belief that they were to he employed in an insurrectionary attempt in Italy. As to M. Bernard, the respect I owe to truth does not permit me io affirm that I have not told him that the hoinbs were to be employed in France, but 1 i cannot still assert that I told liiui so. 1 oftener conversed with him about Italy than about I France.

This exposition of his plans ivas made by the prisoner with the utmost caluiuess ; there was uotliing inflated in his tone, and there appeared little or no affectation in his manner. Orsini related his first meeting with Pierri, and then i with Rudio and Gomez. BeiDg pressed on this point he refused to say more. He merely avowed his participation in the transport of the bombs I and the fulminating powder. On arriving at the events of the 14th his voice, which was before strong and firm, appeared to falter. He avowed the meeting of the accomplices in the Rue Monthabor, aud their proceeding to the Rue Lepelletier. He denied it was he who gave the order to throw the bombs. He himself would not have thrown any. The one he was to throw was given by him to another Italian whose name and co-operation he bad concealed from his accomplices. Wounded by the first explosion he had lost his sight, and it was he who, before entering

The remaiks of the þÿ Tidende are applicable to our Island, and we therefore Lope they w ill meet with some att, ntiou in certain quartern The subject was brought before the notice of the public by a member of the Burgher Council of St. Thomas, moving that representation be made to the Presidency for the purpose of effecting a change in the charges for graves, in order that the Country Treasury may become a participant therein. It was meanwhile decided that the Wardens and Sexton of the Danish Lutheran church be requested to state the amount of fees derived from this source for the last five years. These gentlemen replied in true þÿ circumlocution style, (whether respectfully þÿ that they do not deem themselves authorized or not we do not undertake to say,) to afford the required statement to any other þÿauthority than the þÿPresidency. We trust that this motion will result in some good ; for we heartily agree with the þÿ þÿTidende that the question ought not to be whether the Country Treasury should share the spoils or not, but that the dead, in this respect, should, both there and hue, cease to he a source of revenue to either Church or Treasury

From the St Thomas Times, April 10. We seldom care to make allusion to any portion of the proci edingg published by the Burgher Council, explanatory of the duties devolving on that body, supposing that the community is sufficiently competent to judge of the same. We shall however for once take occasion to remain on a (.art vf its labours, and expri ss ourselves on a question which lias arisen in the Council, with regard to obtaining a proportion of the revenues deriv.-d from the i unal grounds. We commend the Conn il tin its endeavour to secure for its Treasury a part of any revenues arising out of the public ; l ot, in this case, we rattier thick that the more laudable course it could have pursued would have been by using its mos: - rs vering forts to do away altogether with e plan > f tl e þÿ burial þÿgruuiuls' being made sour' i of revenue. It is a poor affair at i. >1 i the living -eek to iive out of the dead ! there >8 but one class of men who may claim urh a light, and they even are held by the mil code under restraint, for the student, if caught in the act of procuring material for the dissecting room, is punishable ; yet his case may be paliated, by knowing that he seeks to possess knowledge out of the dead in order to i benefit the living. With such exception only wo think that the dead should be treated as such, and not made, as in ton many instances, a source of painful reflection to the remaining relatives with scanty means to devine in what manner the expenses for a grave are to be paid, short of asking for one as a pauper. We

all know that it is the Communal money which buys the land, and the Communal money that þÿpay sfor the walls that enclose it, when it s to he converted into a cemetery ; surely, aft. these excessive expenses are gone into from the taxes raised out of the public, nothing more should he looked for than that the cemetery should be self supporting, and that it should be seen as cnntrarv to a Christian principle to at tempt to make a place sanctified by being the receptacle of the dead as a place of revenue If the cemeteries w. re left to support themselves, we should not only find a very great reduction in the charges made to the rich, but the poor would be spared the pain of exposing i'. whilst there would remain, from a small fee, ample means to improve and embclish them, whereas now they are a mass of weeds and briars.

In Mexico they have found less puissant defenders of the hearth and home ; and j upon the north-eastern provinces of that uuhappv country, the Comanehes have been for the last j half-century in the habit of making an annual j foray of war and plunder. In fact, this has be- j come the better part of their subsistence, as they usually return from their rieving expeditions laden with spoil, and carrying with them vast droves of horses, mules, horned cattle, and captive 1 women. For a short time, these dusky freebooters were at peace with the Anglo-American colonists of Texas It was but a temporary armistice, brought about by Houston ; but Lamar's administration, of a less pacific character, succeeded, and the settlers were again embroiled with the Indians. War to the knife was declared and carried on ; red and white killed each other on sight. When two men met npon the prairie, the colour of the skin determined the relations between them ! If they differed in

this, they wore enemies without parley, and to kill the other was the first thought of each. The j lex talionis was the custom of the hour. If the rancour could possibly have been aug- j mented, an incident bad just transpired ealeu- j latcd to have that effect. A band of Comanche I warriors had offered their services to the coin- \ mander-in-chief of the American army! They held the following language : þÿ Let us fight on vonr side We have n quarrel with you. You arc warriors: we know it. and respect you. We fight against the ! cowardly Mexicans, who robbed us of our country. We fight for þÿMoctezuma! These words, uttered along the whole northern frontier of Mexico, are. full of strauge import. The American commander prudently declined \ the Comanche alliance; and the result was the bitter triangular war in which, as already noticed, we were now engaged If, then, the approaching horsemen were In- j dians of the Comanche tribe. þÿRube forecast s was correct ; we had got to fight þÿ With this understanding, wo lost no time in putting ourselves in an attitude of detenoe. and it was full ten miles off. The only thing likely to be met with near the mesa was a warparty of Comanehes, and we knew the Mexicans well enough to be convinced that, whether soldiers or freebooters, they were not in search of that. Buch reflections, made in double-quick time, occurred to us as we scanned the advancing troop. IF ) THE SUGAli ESTATE 66 CAMP ANA 55 The owners of this line Estate having resolved to dispose of the same, possession whereof can be given at the purchaser s option, either immediately or at the conclusion of the present crop. This Estate has been established but very recently, and is-'situated in one of the most fertile parts of the Island of Vieques ; it is about a quarter of an hour's journey distant from the town, and has a good road which communicates with Porto Negro, its port for shipment. It contains about 1,200 cuordas, whereof 200 are planted in Canes, 100 in pasturage, and the remainder in Virgin Forest containing the choicest kinds of wood for building purposes. In addition to some slaves, the Estate has an establishment of about GO free labourers who are bound by contract for one and two years, subject to a renewal ; the great advantages of comfort and an abundant supply of water renders it peculiarly favorable to the wants of the free labourers of the place; in addition to being well found in all respects as a complete Estate, there are two fine Mills, one worked by steam of 12 horse power, the other a Cattle Mill ; the works are supplied with Clarifiers and a spare Boiler, so that in case of accident there can be no suspension of work. The pasturage supports 50 yoke of working Cattle, and in addition to the natural Springs, there is a Cistern ot about 900 puncheons. Twenty-three new wooden Houses tor labourers, residences for Masters and Overseers, Boiling and Curing House, Carts ;

Paris, March Is, 1858 Risorgern ne.nico ognor pi u crudo, Centre ail o sepolta e s pi i to ignudo." (1 shall revive from the dead a still more cruel foe, though but buried ashes and a naked spirit.) These two lines of Tasso's Jerusalem, which Orsini, after Favre's speech, with a strange, smile, whispered to his defender, are already beginning to be fulfilled. The attitude of the crowd witnessing the death of the Italian patriot is thus described by an eyewitness : Such has been the alarm of the Government that an entire division was had out, under the personal command of a general officer, who assisted at the execution. Fifteen thousand soldiers were ready to act on the slightest signal, and every issue and outlet was guarded as in times of insurrection. In my estimation beiween 90,000 and 1 00, 000 men of the Faubourgs, workmen in blouses, were assembled in the spaces and in the streets near the Place de la Roquctte ; but they were so grouped by the way in which the troops were stationed, that thev could sec little or nothing. When the dead, dull sound of the falling of the knil'e upon Orsini was heard, it was responded to by an immense but smothered reply of ' l ire la llepublique' 1 cannot properly describe this; it was like a gigantic mutter ; it was not a cry or a shout, but it souuded like the breath or the sigli of thousands of human beings. It was well appreciated by the authorities, for, on the

instant, the soldiers raised the most disorderly clatter imaginable, struck their horses, so as to make them plunge and kick, shook their arms, and contrived that the popular whisper should he stifled without being literally put down. Hut the words ' ire la llepublii/uc'1 must have been clearly audible to every one. 1 purposely went home on foot, threading my way slowly through the groups wherever I found thein thickest. I am hound to admit that everywhere 1 hoard expressions of sympathy and admiration for Orsini, whose crinm seems utterly forgotten, while only the effect produced by his courage and generosity toward his associates remains. Pierri's name I did not hear once. The attitude of the populace' was 1

marks of a hate and a thirst for vengeance seated too deep for words. All the remarks 1 heard were made in an under tone, as though a police spy were dreaded at every instant. '' It seems, then, that the measures of gene '' can clement, ral safety" intended to weed out the Ilepubli the wholesale imprisonments and transportation, prove no more successful than the ales ouvrieres , the newly-established workshops, and other attempts to purchase the conscience of the French working classes. The circumstances dwelt upon on a former occasion, which accompanied Orsini's trial, have now become the general topic of Paris conversation It, has even oozed out that when the voluminous correspondence of Orsini and Pierri raino to bo examined, letters written by Louis Napoleon, and signed by himself, dated many years ago, came to light If the French Con-

T C; fl 0 I X A y I s stitutionnel was still in the agreeable position it held in Mr. Guizot's time, we should, day after day, be treated with the solemn phrase, " Uhorizon politique s\>bscurat,v And so it does, indeed. Great was the consternation at the Tuileries on ascertaining the conduct of the officers, of the garrison at Chalons, and excessive the anger at the naivete of the Monitenr informing France and Europe that, instead of on the instant laughing at the whole affair, ordering out their men, or declaring that, even were the Republic proclaimed in Paris, they would fight against it for the Empire, the officers at Chalons first ran to the sub-prefect and declined to risk their skins and their commissions for the Emperor, before having made j sure whether or not the Republic was proclaimed. The fact proves tlmt the mass of the army cannot he relied upon. .Save its heads, which are too deeply compromised or have received too brilliant rewards to separate their destinies from that of the Empire, there is perhaps but one single portion of it altogether trustworthy, namely, the Guards. This corps is indeed very strong, and must be aware that, under any other government, it would be merged into the line, or altogether disbanded. Its infantry force consists of four regiments of grenadiers, I two regiments of voltigeurs, one regiment of gens d'aruies, one regiment of Zouaves and | one battalion of chasseurs þÿ altogether seventeen battalions of infantry. It musters, besides. two regiments of cuirassiers, two regi-

ments of dragoons, one regiment of mounted grenadiers, one regiment of hussars, and one regiment of chasseurs, or twenty-one squadrons of cavalry ; its artillery, too, being rather strong Its whole numerical force amounts to about 0,000 men, with 40 to 50 cannons, a nucleus sufficiently powerful to counteract the tendencies to vacillation which might prevail in the line in the case of a serious struggle with the Paris people. Moreover, everything is provided for a sudden concentration of the j troops from the provinces, as the most superficial glance at a railway map of France will prove, so that a movement which should not take the Government by surprise is sure to find I arrayed against it the formidable force of from j 60,000 to 80,000 men But the very measures j Bonaparte lias taken to suppress an armed revolt, make it quite improbable that it should | occur except on some great unforeseen occasion, when the decidedly anti-Bonapartist attitude of the bourgeoisie, the secret societies undermining the lower strata of the army, the petty jealousies, venal treacheries and Orleanist or Legitimist leanings dividing its superior layers, are likely to turu the scale in favor of the revolutionary masses. The worst thing j that could happen to the latter would be a successful attempt on Bonaparte's life. In that case the answer given by Morny, at the beginning of the Russian war, to Bonaparte's question, what '' they intended doing on his sud- den dealtli : Nous commenrerions de jeler tous

" les Jeromes par lefeuetre, et puis nous tacheri- ' ons de nous arranger taut bun que mal avec les 1 ' Orleans. " We shall begin by throwing all the Jeromes out of the window, and then we shall arrange matters as well as wo can with the Orleans family, | would perhaps turn out a prophecy. Before the men of the faubourgs could have decided upon the course to take, Morny might execute his palace-revolution, proclaim the Orleans, and thus draw over the middle classes to the anti-revolutionary camp. Meanwhile Bonaparte's disappointments in the field of foreign policy vastly contribute to should say, extremely menacing, for it had the I virga him on in his system of domestic terror ism. Every check he sustains from without, by betraying the weakness of his position, and giving new life to the aspirations of bis antagonists, is necessarily followed tip by new displays j of what is called "governmental vigor." And these foreign miscarriages have rapidly accumulated during the last weeks. There was first the great failure with regard to England. Then even Switzerland, although she lias made very cowardly concessions, took courage to demur at the further steps urged upon her in the most unceremonious manner. It was formally declared to the Confederation that, if necessary, regiments of French infantry would enter and perform those police duties which the police of Switzerland could not do for themselves. At this point even Mr. Kern lound it necessary to demand his passports, and the French Government to draw off. Bel
gitlin. having altered its law at Bonaparte's

dictation, declined to comply with the demand for Gen. Changarnier's expulsion. The Commission of the Piedmontese Chamber charged with the duty of examining the bill to assimilate the Sardinian institutions to the Idees Napoleonitnnes, bv a majority of five against two, proposed the pure and simple rejection of the Bouapartist project. Austria, fully aware that Orsini's execution has bound over to her, hand and foot, the hero of Strasburg, and that lie can no longer alarm her through Italy, shows him the cold shoulder To expose itself to ridicule is the surest way for a French Government to annihilate it-elt" Bonaparte is conscious of the grotesque luster which his be baffled attempts at playing the dictator f Europe have sheajupon him. The more contemptible bis European position grows, the more keenly he feels the necessity of appearing formidable to France. Consequently, the reign of terror is progressively extending. Gen Espinassc, at the bead of the Ministry of the Interior, is now backed by Mi Boitelle, a former colonel in the hussars, at the head of the Prefecture of Police. The system adopted by these military myrmidons of the second Empire is thus described in The Continental llei iew : " They have taken the old lists of individuals who, after the troubles of 1S48 and 1851, were designated by the police as dangerous, and they have arrested these persons en masse, both in Paris and in the departments. All this was done without the slightest inquiry being made

as to whether or not these persons had since that period given ground of complaint, and the most cruel effects have ensued. Thus, honest citizens, who, being carried away in 184S by the whirlwind which agitated the whole nation, professed advanced ideas, but who have since abandoned politics, and many of whom are now fathers of families and industrious tradesmen, were carried off by the police from the inidst of their affairs and from their families. These are known facts which show how little ground there was for the arrests, and with what an absence of even the semblance of legality or necessity these measures of terrorism were carried out. Among the persons whom the agents of the police attempted to arrest, there were some individuals who had been no less than six years out of France, and who consequently could not have committed any offence hut who, if they had been in France at the present moment, would inevitably have been thrown into prison on pretense of 'public safety.' Nay, more, the police went to the houses of several persons who had been dead for some years, for the purpose of arresting tlicin. Their names figured on the lists of persons formerly arrested (and many of these simply because they were among the crowd in the streets, and t lint was their only crime.) It is therefore clear that it, is not against the guilty that the police war, hut against the suspected ; and the manner in which the law is executed is of itself a justification of the title conferred upon it by public opinion. In the

departments matters proceed pretty much as in 1'aris. The lists of the suspected were drawn up by the administrative authorities, and woe to those who, in the elections of June last, ventured to oppose the candidates supported by the Prefect, and who, looking on the Constitution, the electoral law and the circulars of the Minister of the Interior as serious realities, have believed that they might take measures for the election of the candidates of their choice. These latter are considered ns the worst of culprits, and they must be either very rich; very influential, or very well protected by their friends, to escape the vengeance of those officials whose paths they had crossed. Among the persons arrested in the provinces appears . played a part in 148 as Commander-in-Chief the name of Gen. Courtais, who, after having of the National Guard of Paris, lived for the last nine years in the greatest retirement in a country house in the department of the Allier, removed from society, and altogether a stranger to politics or public affairs." What with this system of " general safety," what with the pangs of a commercial crisis that lias become chronic, the French middle classes will soon he worked up to the point where they will consider a revolution necessary for the " restoration of confidence."

GRANADA, 30 th March, 185s Passage of the Treaty. Since writing the above, I have learned of the passage of the Uass-Yrizzari Treaty, it was ratified contrary to all expectation on Sa turday, the. 28th inst. Several of the members opposed to it were absent, and the opportunity was embraced to liave it through. The members from Leon went for it in a body, but the Granadinos generally opposed it The vote stood ten to five. It was opposed by Dr. Falla, Pedro Chamorro, Jose Antonio Mejia, Pedro Prado, and Francisco J intones. The Treaty is very popular in Leon, but in Granada. Massaya, and Rivas, the gent are indignant at its passage. I have read the document embracing about thirty articles, and these are the chief features ; The l nited States is empowered to open, and keep open the Transit. San Juan del Norte and Sail Juan del Slid to be free ports : Americans to be allowed to live in the country, marry, and hold real estate, without taking the oath of allegiance to the State of Nicaragua A þÿ .INFRtlAMNESTY TOWARDS ALL AMI. CL ANS American merchants to be allowed to intro liuce their goods at the same rates as those which native merchants pay. The United States to he allowed to place troops on the Transit, when it (the United States) shall deem it necessary for the security of the same. The Ship Canal or Railroad to be considered under American protection. Colonizers who buy land and settle in the country, and take allegiance to the same, to he protected by the United States, if Nicaragua

fails to do so. The United States to be allowed to disembark forces &e., for the maintenance of a naval station. All Americans taking the oath of allegiance, to become instantly citizens FREEDOM OF SFF.ECH AND RELIGIOUS OmioN. The United States to protect the Transit (i. e. the State), against all foreign invasion, and to maintain internal quietude American citizens naturalized or otherwise to have all civil rights in quality with native Nicaraguans. There arc many other provisions of an interesting character but as I have but a moment to write, I cannot enumerate them all. The American Eagle lias taken a long sweep over the Cordilleras, and every true American will feel a thrill of joy at this consummation. þÿVanderbilt sprospects are nearly fallen to the ground The day of the ratification of the Treaty the Assembly granted an extension
of time to November, to the White Stubbing Company. Lamar has had au open row with his Secretary, and discharged him.

In perfect coolness, we regarded them þÿ at least so much can I say for my comrades Though life or death rested upon the issue, both were as coot at that moment as if they had been ouly observing the movements of a gang of buffalot There was no sign ot trepidation hardly a symptom of excitement visible in the countenance of either. Now and then, a half-muttered ejaculation, a rapid exchange of thought, relating to some fresh movement of the enemy, alone told that both were alive to the peril of the situation. 1 cannot affirm that I shared with them this extreme and perfect sang froid ; though upon my nerves less, indifferent to danger, their example had its effect, and inspired me with courage sufficient for the occasion. Besides, I drew confidence from another source In case of defeat, 1 had a resource unshared by my companions þÿ perhaps unthought of by them. Trusting to tne matchless speed of my horse, as a last j resort, I might possibly escape. I could have ridden off at that moment without fear of being overtaken, hut the craven thought was not entertained for an instant. By my honour, no ! I should have accepted death upon the spot rather than desert the brave men who stood by my side. To them 1 was indebted for my life. | þÿ Twasfor me that theirs were now in peril ; and

from the first moment l had determined to stand by them to the end, and sell my blood at its dearest. In the event of both falling before me, it would then be time to think of flight. Even this contingency had the effect o strengthening my courage, and at that moment 1 viowed the vengeful foe with a coolness and freedom from fear that now, in the retrospect, surprises me. During the interval of inaction that followed, I was cool enough to reflect upon the demand which the guerrilla leader had made þÿ the surrender of my person. Why was I singled out? We were all enemies alike þÿ ail Americans or Texans on Mexican soil, and armed for þÿ strife. Why they did want me alone ? Was it because I was superior in rank to my companions ' But how knew they this ? þÿ how knew they I was a þÿ ranger captain 91 Ha 1 they must have known it before ; they must have come out specially in search of me ! A light flashed suddenly into my mind þÿ a suspicion strong almost as certainty. But for the sun glancing in my eyes, I might have earlier obtained an explanation of the mystery. I drew down the visor of my forage-cap, stretching it to its full extent; I increased the shade with my flattened palms, and from under them strained my eyes upon the leader of the band. Already his voice, while in conversation with Garcy, had aroused a faint recollection within me. 1 had j these heard that voice only once, but I thought l remembered it. Guided by my suspicion, I now , before ub like the scrutinised more closely the face of the man.

Fortunately, it was turned towards me, and despite the dazzling of the sunbeam, despite the slouched sombrero, I reoognised the dark features of Rafael Ijurra ! In that glance I comprehended the situation He it was who wanted the þÿ ranger yielding captain þÿ! There was doubt no longer. My suspicion was a certainty ; but with the next turob of my heart rose another, thousand a times more painful þÿ -a suspicion of With an effort, 1 stifled my emotions ; a move- , ment was perceptible among the guerrilleros ; the moment of action had arrived ! Irregularly grouped, they exhibited a þÿ clump upon the prairie, some standing still, others in niotioD- As Rube uttered the last words, one of them was seen to shoot out from the body, spurring his steed into a gallop as he parted from the crowd. One might have fancied he was about to ride j horse, off from the ground : but no ; that was not his intention. YVhen he had made half-a-dozen stretches over the plain, he guided his horse into | ' barrel of the instantly a curve, evidently with the design of riding around us. As soon as he had gained some score of yards from the troop, a second horseman followed, repeating the manoeuvre ; and then another and another, until five of the band thus deployed, galloped round us in circles The remaining six kept their ground. YY'e observed that the five had left their lances behind them, and carried only their carbines. þÿYV e were not astonished at this : we divined the intention of our enemies. They were about to practise an old prairie-tactic þÿ a stratagem of the horse-Indians, with which all three of us

were familiar. We might have been more apprehensive about the result had it been really Indians who were going to practise the manoeuvre þÿ since in an at tack of this kind, the bow, with its many missiles in a minute, is far more dangerous than either carbine or rifle. But the fact that our assailants understood the stratagem, told us we were opposed to men who had seen lndian-fight þÿ no doubt, the piok men of the frontier þÿ and to defend ourselves would require all the courage and cunuing we possessed. It did not surprise us that only a portion of the band galloped out to effect the surround ; there was design iu that, and wc knew it. The five who had been detached were to wheel round us in circles, dash at intervals within range, fire their carbines, kill some of our horses, keep us distracted, and, if possible, draw the fire of our rifles. This purpose effected, the other six þÿ who had already approached as near as was safe for them þÿ would charge forward, empty their guns, and then use their lazocs with effect. Of this last weapon my companions had more dread than all the others carried by our foes. They had reason. They knew that our rifles once empty, the lazo could be used beyond pistol-range ; and by such men, with far surer aim than either carbine or cscopette ! We were allowed but scant time to entertain doubts, fears, and conjectures, or to communicate them to one another. They passed I lightning's flash : the quicker that they were old thoughts things þÿ familiar |

from experience. We were conscious that the stratagem of our enemy had increased the peril i of our situation; hut we thought not yet of to despair In an instant we had altered our relative positions The three of us no longer fronted in one direction, but stood back to back þÿ each to guard 1 þÿYVhat to the third of the circle before his face. Thus stood we, rifles in hand. The five horsemen were not slow in the execution of their manoeuvre. Once or twice they galloped round us in a wide circle ; and and nearer. following a spiral curve, drew nearer then YVhen within carbine range, eaoh fired his piece ; I the flappin þÿo a þÿbeaver tail, and, retreating outward upon the main body, 1 none þÿ0 the sooplest. Tnr no þÿuse. hastily exchanged his empty gun for one that was loaded, and galloped back as before. In the first volley, most of their bullets, discharged at random, had passed over our heads. YVTe heard them hissing in the air high above us. One, however, had been better aimed, and struck Rube's mare in the hip, causing the old mustang to squeal and kick violently It did but little damage, though it was an earnest of what we þÿ Cowardly þÿskunks! muttered Rube; þÿ they might expect ; and it was with increased apprehension that we saw the horsemen come back on their circling career.

You will wonder why we did not return their fire ? Our guns carried as far as theirs, Why did wc not use them, while the horsemen were within range ? Not one of the three of us thought of drawing a trigger ! You will wonder at this? It requires explanation. Know, then, that the five men who galloped round us were five of the best horsemeD in the world þÿ no doubt the picked riders of the band, j Not in Arabia, not in the hippodromes of Paris or London, could they have found their superiors þÿ perhaps not their equals, for these men literally lived in the saddle. RUSSIA. A dispatch from 8t. Petersburg says the Russian Government is at the present moment watching with great interest the relations between England and France. The Russian navy this summer is to be fully manned, and ship-building increased to a great extent. Russia has 110 intention of accepting English and French consuls in the Black Soa. A letter from Warsaw, of March 21, states that a camp of 100,000 men will be formed there towards the middle of May. This measure is considered to he a manifestation against Austria. A great agitation prevails in Russia, in consequence of the opposition of the nobility to the emancipation of the serfs. Many great proprietors have fled to St. Petersburg in fear of their lives.

EMEUTE AT CHALONS. The Iiloniteur of Tuesday publishes the following in its non-official columns : þÿ " At Clialons-sur-Saone on Saturday night, about 9 o'clock, some 40 individuals suddenly attacked a small post of infantry, which they took by surprise They then took the direction of the railway station, shouting 'Vive la Rt publique !' 'The Republic is proclaimed in Paris!' 'The Republic is everywhere!' 'Citizens of Chalons to arms !' The station-master, an old soldier, assembled the men employed at the railway station, and drove back the rioters From the railway station the mob proceeded to the bridge over the Saone, the head of which they occupied to prevent an alarm being sent to the barracks. The officers of the garrison, who had hurried to the Sous-Prefecture to ascertain what the (umult was about, cleared the bridge sword in hand. The troops turned out, and the mob dispersed. Before midnight 15 of the more conspicuous ringleaders were in custody." The correspondent of the Times writes on Tuesday : þÿ " The paragraph in the Moniteur describing the revolt of about 40 men at Cha 1 ons-sur-Soane, who surprised the military post to the cry of ' Vive la Republique !' has puz zled people a good deal Chalons is not so far from Paris that a handful of men could hope to persuade an entire population that the Government was overthrown and the Republic restored throughout France. And then the officers, it appears, first ra (the Momtmr says) to the house ol the Sub-Prefect to know if the news

was true, and, when they found it was not, forced their passage, sword in hand, to the bar racks There arc various conjectures on this subject, exaggerated, no doubt, and contradictory One is, that the affair was more serious than is represented, and that the resi.-tanco was greater Another account is, that the eehavffiouru was only an attempt to rescue some persons who had been arrested under the new I'enal Law, and who were in the act of being taken off. Nothing is more likely than that the friends of the arrested raised a clamour, and that those who are ready to profit by every opportunity increased the disturbance." Marshal Castellane had arrived at Chalons, he quitted, Lyons, where he commands, the moment the news reached him. The Patrit publishes further particulars. It says þÿ " Wo have received from Chalons-sur Saone some new details relative to the revolutionary attempt of which that city was the. scene on the evening of the 6th. Favoured by the darkness and by a heavy fall of .now, the. rioters, prec-ded by some individua's of an inoffensive appearance, proceeded first to a small infantry post in the Rue de Bcaunes, At some distance oft the majority of the mob halted ; those who formed a soit of adva er> guard went up to the sentinel, who was instantly surrounded and disarmed in spite of his resistance, while one of the assailants put his hand on his mouth to prevent his raising an alarm. After this first success the remainder of the rioters rapidly advanced on the guard.

The soldiers, half asleep, could not prevent the seizure of the arms which were placed in the gun-rack near the door, but the Serjeant in command had time to draw bis sword and seize a few of the muskets, which he distributed amongst bis men, ordering them to load immc diately. The rioterrs, who had possessed them selves of arms, then left the post, and went to the railway station, where, as the Moniteur announced, they were energetically repulsed.
